claims.claim: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin developed the three-point seatbelt and filed its patent in 1959 (U.S. patent 3,043,625, filed August 1959).
claims.episode_span: The three-point seatbelt itself was the work of Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin, who filed the patent in 1959 after studying crash data
claims.supporting_quote: After testing the three-point safety belt, he introduced his invention to the Volvo company in 1959 and received his first patent (number 3,043,625).

claims.claim: Sam Peltzman published "The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation" in the Journal of Political Economy in 1975, arguing that risk compensation offset the benefits of federal auto safety standards.
claims.episode_span: University of Chicago professor Sam Peltzman published a 1975 paper arguing that earlier federal safety standards had already produced measurable risk compensation
claims.supporting_quote: who published "The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation" in the Journal of Political Economy in 1975 in which he controversially suggested that "offsets (due to risk compensation) are virtually complete, so that regulation has not decreased highway deaths"

claims.claim: Peltzman's 1975 analysis argued the offset was essentially complete, so that regulation had not decreased highway deaths.
claims.episode_span: Peltzman’s analysis argued the offset was essentially complete — in his words, the net number of driver fatalities was unaffected by the mandates.
claims.supporting_quote: who published "The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation" in the Journal of Political Economy in 1975 in which he controversially suggested that "offsets (due to risk compensation) are virtually complete, so that regulation has not decreased highway deaths"

claims.claim: Later empirical work found risk-compensation effects exist in many contexts but generally offset less than half of the direct safety benefit.
claims.episode_span: Later studies of belt laws produced smaller but still detectable offsets—estimates ranging from 10 to 40 percent of the lifesaving effect
claims.supporting_quote: Substantial further empirical work has found that the effect exists in many contexts but generally offsets less than half of the direct effect.

claims.claim: Risk compensation by belted drivers can redistribute injury risk onto people outside the vehicle, such as pedestrians and cyclists.
claims.episode_span: Because the offset fell most heavily on people outside the vehicle, the net social benefit remained strongly positive
claims.supporting_quote: if a risk-tolerant driver responds to driver-safety interventions, such as compulsory seat belts , crumple zones , anti-lock brakes , etc., by driving faster with less attention, then this can result in increases in injuries

claims.claim: The Australian state of Victoria made seat belt wearing compulsory in 1970, the world's first such mandate.
claims.episode_span: Australia’s state of Victoria led the way with the world’s first mandatory-wearing law in December 1970; belt use rose quickly and driver death rates fell.
claims.supporting_quote: the use of seat belts by all vehicle passengers was made compulsory in the states of Victoria and South Australia in 1970 and 1971, respectively.

claims.claim: New York passed the first U.S. state law mandating seat belt use, in 1984.
claims.episode_span: In the United States, New York’s 1984 law was followed by more than thirty states within five years.
claims.supporting_quote: New York State passed the first law in the US mandating the use of seat belts in 1984 under the leadership of John D. States

claims.claim: New Hampshire is the only U.S. state with no law requiring adults (over 18) to wear a seat belt.
claims.episode_span: Today every U.S. state except New Hampshire requires adult belt use, and observed wearing rates exceed 90 percent in most places.
claims.supporting_quote: with the exception of New Hampshire, which does not have a law requiring people over age 18 to wear a seat belt.

claims.claim: U.S. seat belt use rose from 14% in the early 1980s to about 90% by 2016.
claims.episode_span: Today every U.S. state except New Hampshire requires adult belt use, and observed wearing rates exceed 90 percent in most places.
